questions.q: What is Maitland's first suggestion for getting more solitude?
a: Extend the solo activities you already do
Book a silent retreat for a month
Cut off contact with your friends
Move to a remote countryside cottage
questions.why: Lesson one says to start by doing more or longer sessions of things you already do alone, like running or walking.

questions.q: Why don't music, books or films count as real solitude?
a: You are still engaging with another person's work
They cost money and require planning
They are too distracting to relax you
They always involve other people nearby
questions.why: The summary says that even alone, you are connecting with the creator rather than with your own thoughts.

questions.q: Which childhood activity does solitude help adults recover?
a: Daydreaming and letting the imagination wander
Sleeping deeply through the night
Playing team sports with friends
Learning new languages quickly
questions.why: Lesson two says reverie and active imagination brought many of us joy as children and can do so again.

questions.q: What did Carl Jung find when he reviewed his happiest childhood memories?
a: They came from imagining while alone
They came from family holidays abroad
They came from winning at school
They came from time with close friends
questions.why: The summary says Jung's notes showed most of his happiest memories came from using his imagination alone.

questions.q: What is Maitland's view of the introvert versus extrovert labels?
a: They are useless because people shift with context
Introverts need far more solitude than extroverts
Extroverts should force themselves to be alone
The labels predict how much solitude you need
questions.why: Lesson three says everyone is both depending on the situation, so psychology should not decide your ideal dose of solitude.
